item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"NAD/NADP binding is not a single evolutionary signature. In the current public SCOPe release, 2.08, NAD(P)-bearing annotations appear in several unrelated places in the hierarchy: the superfamilies c.2.1, NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains; c.3.1, FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain; c.25.1, Ferredoxin reductase-like C-terminal NADP-linked domain; and c.31.1, DHS-like NAD/FAD-binding domain all sit in different folds within class c, while d.58.20, the NAD-binding domain of HMG-CoA reductase, is under the Ferredoxin-like fold in class d, and e.52.1, NAD kinase/diacylglycerol kinase-like, is in a multidomain class-e fold. SCOPe's homology endpoint marks these superfamily nodes as homology-implying, but marks the fold nodes themselves as above the level where homology is implied; therefore ancestry can be inferred within a family or supported superfamily, not merely between any two proteins that bind NAD(P), share the same broad class, or even have a related cofactor-binding fold. The biological implication is a mixture of divergence and convergence: members of a given family, and usually of a SCOPe superfamily, can be treated as divergent relatives, but the repeated use of NAD(P) or flavin/NAD chemistry across distinct SCOPe folds is convergent recruitment of the same cofactor chemistry onto different scaffolds. Cofactor binding and local active-site resemblance are unsafe homology tests by themselves because NAD(P) imposes similar phosphate/ribose/adenine/nicotinamide geometry, short glycine-rich or polar binding motifs can recur, and a few catalytic residues can be placed analogously without a common domain ancestor. Function transfer and template use should therefore be limited to globally supported homologous domains, ideally the same family or a well-supported same-superfamily match over the conserved core; one NAD(P)-binding representative or template from c.2.1 should not be used as evidence to annotate, model, or transfer substrate specificity to c.3.1, c.25.1, d.58.20, or e.52.1 merely because the ligand or reaction chemistry looks similar.
